extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in social theory, public health, health policy, media studies; journalists and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of how obesity is represented in public and scientific discourse, highlighting ethical issues, methodological uncertainties, and the social/political consequences of those representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge scientific uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Public and media representations should reflect the many uncertainties, ambiguities and contradictions in the primary research on obesity rather than issuing claims with unwarranted authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/editors/reporters should avoid presenting tentative or contested findings as settled facts; explicitly state methodological limitations, gaps in knowledge, and conflicting evidence (eg. the tenuous links between weight and health noted by Gard and Wright, Flegal, etc.). Anti-pattern: recycling 'scientific evidence' in ways that belie uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating overweight with obesity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat overweight (measured by weight/BMI) as synonymous with obesity (excess fat); using overweight as a proxy for obesity exaggerates the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify conceptual differences and measurement limits. Example: Brownell notes weight is easy to measure but fat is not; using weight as proxy can mislead prevalence estimates and policy responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on BMI as sole index of health
rubrics_metrics.description: BMI focuses only on weight (kg/m2) and may misclassify muscular or athletic people and is a poor index for children/adolescents; it tells little about actual health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measures that capture body fat and consider fitness/activity levels; when using BMI, explicitly state its limitations and avoid treating chart cutoffs as precise individual health determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make social determinants visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Include socio-cultural and socio-economic factors when discussing causes and solutions for obesity rather than privileging purely biomedical explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize individual behaviours within structural factors (poverty, food environments, class). Use evidence like Whitehall studies showing mortality risk linked to social factors; avoid 'body-as-machine' simplifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid universalizing thinness as a moral/health imperative
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist messaging that presents thinness or weight loss as a universal good for everyone; such universalism ignores individual, cultural and physiological differences and can be ethically problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question assumptions that losing weight benefits all; note evidence that moderate overweight + activity may be healthier than thin + sedentary. Anti-pattern: policies/education that demand 'thinness for all' without nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid individualizing and moralizing frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not primarily frame obesity as an individual's moral failing (lazy, greedy) or place sole responsibility on personal choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance individual behavior change narratives with systemic/environmental explanations. Media should not manufacture moral panic that stigmatizes people; avoid language that pathologizes bodily difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider ethical consequences of discourse (stigma, shame, identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how obesity discourse shapes social identities, produces guilt and shame, and can precipitate disordered relationships with food and the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly discuss potential harms of messaging (e.g., increased eating disorders, isolation). Anti-patterns include excluding moral/ethical reflection from public health communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report risk and relative risk responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Media and public texts should accurately represent relative and absolute risks and avoid exaggerated or alarmist framings of risk that produce availability heuristics and moral panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify risk carefully, cite uncertainty, and avoid sensational headlines (examples from tabloids provided). Frost et al.'s work on media misrepresentation of relative risk is a relevant guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish scientific/technical expertise from ethical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: When experts are quoted, distinguish between technical scientific claims and ethical or moral commentary; invite ethical debate rather than letting scientific authority uncritically carry moral judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media and policymakers should include ethicists or social theorists where moral dimensions are implicated. Miah (2005) argues for ethical engagement with science to contextualize findings for non-experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report methodological limitations and call for better questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When research is critiqued, go beyond calls for 'better trials' and consider whether the framing/questions themselves need revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reflexive solutions that only demand improved behaviour-change techniques; assess whether the underlying assumptions (eg. weight as the key variable) are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and report harms/limitations of weight-loss programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge low success rates and potential adverse effects (metabolic harm, increased binge eating, psychological harms) associated with many weight-loss interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss evidence (eg. Aphramor on 95% unsuccessful programmes; Olson et al. on adverse metabolic effects) and ethical responsibility before promoting aggressive weight-loss policies or programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include alternative humanistic/size-acceptance discourses
rubrics_metrics.description: Give voice to discourses that value body diversity (size/fat acceptance) and research that challenges the assumption that fatness necessarily equals poor health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present findings showing overweight is not necessarily linked to excess mortality (Flegal et al., Gregg et al.) and avoid marginalizing critical social-theory perspectives as merely 'soft' or distracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid policy-driven evidence-seeking (policy looking for evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let pre-existing policy positions determine the interpretation or selection of evidence; avoid using evidence merely to justify policies already favoured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be reflexive about how research is mobilized in policy debates; encourage reframing of questions when evidence is weak or ambiguous (Anderson's observation of 'a policy looking for an evidence base').

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when using alarmist metaphors and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid metaphors (epidemic, plague, war) and dire predictions that moralize and dramatize health problems in ways that may distort public understanding or justify coercive measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, contextualized language to headline-grabbing metaphors; examine House of Commons report examples and tabloid headlines as anti-patterns that feed moral panic.
